prompt: According to Roald Hoffmann's definition, when are two molecular fragments isolobal?

choices.text: When their frontier orbitals are similar in number, symmetry, energy, shape and electron count
When they have the same total number of valence electrons and the same overall structure
choices.why: That describes isoelectronic species. Isolobal fragments need only similar frontier orbitals: 17 VE Mn(CO)5 and 7 VE CH3 are isolobal even though their electron counts differ.

choices.text: When their central atoms belong to the same group of the periodic table and carry the same ligands
choices.why: CH3, NH2 and OH have central atoms from three different groups, yet all three are isolobal, each with one frontier orbital holding one electron.

choices.text: When each fragment already has a complete octet or a complete 18-electron count
choices.why: A fragment with a complete count has no frontier orbitals left for bonding. Isolobal fragments fall short of the stable count by the same amount, which gives them matching frontier orbitals.

explanation: Hoffmann, who won the 1981 Nobel Prize in chemistry, called fragments isolobal ("similar lobes") if the number, symmetry properties, approximate energy and shape of their frontier orbitals, and the number of electrons in them, are similar: not identical, but similar. Isolobal fragments are compatible building blocks, so they will likely form stable bonds with each other.

prompt: Using the octet-based rule for main group fragments, how many frontier orbitals does an NH fragment have?
explanation: NH has 5 + 1 = 6 valence electrons. The number of frontier orbitals, and the number of electrons in them, is 8 − VE = 8 − 6 = 2. So NH has two frontier orbitals holding two electrons, and two NH fragments combine to give diazene, HN=NH.

prompt: By the octet-based rule, which of these is isolobal with a CH2 fragment?

choices.text: An O atom
An OH fragment
choices.why: OH has 7 VE, so it has 8 − 7 = 1 frontier orbital with one electron. It is isolobal with CH3, not CH2.

choices.text: An N atom
choices.why: An N atom has 5 VE and so three frontier orbitals with three electrons. It is isolobal with CH.

choices.text: An NH3 molecule
choices.why: NH3 has 8 VE, so 8 − 8 = 0: it has no frontier orbitals to match the two of CH2.

explanation: CH2 has 4 + 2 = 6 VE, giving 8 − 6 = 2 frontier orbitals with two electrons. An oxygen atom also has 6 valence electrons, so it is isolobal with CH2. Combining the two gives formaldehyde, H2C=O, just as two CH2 fragments give ethene and two O atoms give O2.

prompt: A CH fragment and an N atom both have 5 valence electrons, so they are isolobal. What molecule results from combining them?

choices.text: Hydrogen cyanide, HCN
Methanimine, H2C=NH
choices.why: Methanimine comes from combining the 6 VE fragments CH2 and NH.

choices.text: Diazene, HN=NH
choices.why: Diazene comes from combining two 6 VE NH fragments.

choices.text: Acetylene, C2H2
choices.why: Acetylene comes from two CH fragments. Replacing one CH with an N atom gives H–CN.

explanation: A 5 VE fragment has 8 − 5 = 3 frontier orbitals with three electrons. Two CH fragments give acetylene, C2H2, two N atoms give dinitrogen, N2, and one of each gives H–CN, hydrogen cyanide.

prompt: Using the 18-electron-based rule for organometallic fragments, how many frontier orbitals does the Co(CO)3 fragment have?
explanation: Co contributes 9 valence electrons and each CO contributes 2, so Co(CO)3 has 9 + 3 × 2 = 15 VE. The number of frontier orbitals, and of electrons in them, is 18 − VE = 18 − 15 = 3. A 15 VE carbonyl fragment like Co(CO)3 is therefore isolobal with a 5 VE fragment such as CH.

prompt: Fe(CO)4 is a 16 VE fragment with two frontier orbitals. What do Fe(CO)4 fragments form when they combine with each other?

choices.text: A trimeric cluster, Fe3(CO)12, in which each Fe makes single bonds to the two other Fe atoms
A stable dimer, (CO)4Fe=Fe(CO)4, in which the two Fe atoms share an Fe=Fe double bond
choices.why: Metal–metal double and triple bonds are not formed in carbonyl complexes. The fragments form clusters with single bonds instead.

choices.text: A tetrahedral tetramer, Fe4(CO)16, in which each Fe makes single bonds to three other Fe atoms
choices.why: Three single bonds per metal need three frontier orbitals, as in 15 VE fragments like Co(CO)3. Fe(CO)4 has only two.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because a 16 VE carbonyl fragment has no isolobal partner to bond with
choices.why: Fe(CO)4 is isolobal with the 6 VE fragment CH2, and the two combine to give a carbene complex with an Fe=C double bond.

explanation: The number of single bonds a metal makes equals the number of its frontier orbitals. Each 16 VE Fe(CO)4 fragment has two, so instead of an Fe=Fe double bond, three fragments join into the trimer Fe3(CO)12, each Fe bonded to the other two. A 16 VE fragment can still form a double bond to carbon: Fe(CO)4 plus CH2 gives a carbene complex.

prompt: Combining the 15 VE fragment Co(CO)3 with the 5 VE fragment CH gives a stable complex. Which description fits it?

choices.text: A carbyne complex, with a Co–C triple bond
A carbene complex, with a Co–C double bond
choices.why: Carbene complexes have a metal–carbon double bond, as when a 16 VE fragment combines with CH2. Co(CO)3 and CH each have three frontier orbitals.

choices.text: A μ3-methine complex, with CH bridging three Co atoms
choices.why: In a μ3-methine complex, one CH bonds to three Co(CO)3 fragments, as when one Co(CO)3 of Co4(CO)12 is replaced by CH. Here there is only one Co.

choices.text: An unstable species that has never been isolated
choices.why: It's metal–metal triple bonds, like Co≡Co, that carbonyl fragments avoid. The Co≡C complex is stable.

explanation: Each fragment has three frontier orbitals (18 − 15 = 3 for Co(CO)3 and 8 − 5 = 3 for CH), so together they form (CO)3Co≡CH, with a Co≡C triple bond. Complexes with metal–carbon triple bonds are called carbyne complexes; those with metal–carbon double bonds are carbene complexes. Two Co(CO)3 fragments, by contrast, don't form a stable Co≡Co triple bond.

prompt: Four 15 VE Co(CO)3 fragments join into the tetrahedral cluster Co4(CO)12. How many of its 12 CO ligands are bridging?
explanation: Co4(CO)12 has nine terminal and three bridging CO ligands. The three bridging COs connect the three Co atoms of the base triangular face of the tetrahedron. Each Co uses its three frontier orbitals to make single bonds to the other three Co atoms.

prompt: Co4(CO)12 and Rh4(CO)12 each have three bridging CO ligands, but Ir4(CO)12 has only terminal ones. How does the section explain this?

choices.text: The Ir–Ir bonds are longer than the Co–Co and Rh–Rh bonds
The Ir–Ir bonds are shorter than the Co–Co and Rh–Rh bonds
choices.why: This is reversed. The section links the all-terminal structure to the larger Ir–Ir bond length.

choices.text: Ir has fewer valence electrons than Co and Rh
choices.why: Co, Rh and Ir are all in group 9, so their M(CO)3 fragments all have 15 VE.

choices.text: Ir4(CO)12 is unstable compared with Ir2(CO)8
choices.why: It's the other way around: Ir2(CO)8 is not stable, and Ir4(CO)12 even forms spontaneously from the elements.

explanation: The difference is explained by the larger Ir–Ir bond length. The section gives it as a general rule that bridging CO ligands are found for 3d and 4d metals, while only terminal CO ligands are observed for 5d metals. Unlike Co4(CO)12, which is made by heating Co2(CO)8 above 54 °C, Rh4(CO)12 and Ir4(CO)12 form spontaneously from the elements.

prompt: Which of these carbonyl clusters, each built from isolobal fragments, is known to be stable?

choices.text: Mn3(CO)12^3−, a trimer of 16 VE Mn(CO)4^− fragments
Fe4(CO)12^4−, a tetramer of 15 VE Fe(CO)3^− fragments
choices.why: This cluster is not known. A 4− charge, with each Fe formally 1−, causes too much electrostatic repulsion between the Fe atoms for stable Fe–Fe bonds.

choices.text: Co3(CO)12^3+, a trimer of 16 VE Co(CO)4^+ fragments
choices.why: Each Co would have a coordination number of 6, but a 3+ charge is too high. Stable carbonyl clusters shouldn't carry positive charges.

choices.text: Cr3(CO)15, a trimer of 16 VE Cr(CO)5 fragments
choices.why: Each Cr would be bonded to five CO ligands and two Cr atoms, a coordination number of 7, which is too high for a carbonyl.

explanation: Mn has one electron fewer than Fe, so Mn(CO)4^− is a 16 VE fragment isoelectronic with Fe(CO)4. Its trimer, Mn3(CO)12^3−, is stable: a 3− charge is not yet too high, and each Mn has the ideal coordination number of 6 (four CO plus two Mn). As a rule, stable carbonyl clusters have no positive charges, no high negative charges and no high coordination numbers.

prompt: Fe(CO)4^+ is a 15 VE fragment, so four of them could in principle form a tetrahedral Fe4(CO)16^4+ cluster. Counting both CO ligands and neighboring Fe atoms, what would the coordination number of each Fe be?
explanation: Each Fe would carry four CO ligands and, like the Co atoms in Co4(CO)12, bond to the other three metal atoms of the tetrahedron: 4 + 3 = 7. That is too high for a carbonyl, and the positive charge also destabilizes the Fe–C bonds, so this cluster is not stable. Isolobality is not always enough to make a stable molecule; coordination number and charge matter too.

prompt: Fe3(CO)12 is built from three Fe(CO)4 fragments. If one Fe(CO)4 is replaced by an isolobal CH2 fragment, how many cluster valence electrons (CVE) does the resulting cluster have?
explanation: Fe(CO)4 has 8 + 4 × 2 = 16 VE and CH2 has 4 + 2 = 6 VE. Replacing one Fe(CO)4 gives 2 × 16 + 6 = 38 CVE, down from 3 × 16 = 48. The CH2 bridges the two Fe atoms, so this is a μ-methylene complex. Replacing a second Fe(CO)4 gives a 28 CVE ethene complex, and replacing all three gives cyclopropane.

prompt: In Co4(CO)12, two Co(CO)3 fragments are replaced by isolobal CH fragments, giving a CH–CH unit bonded to two Co(CO)3 fragments. How many cluster valence electrons does the product have?
explanation: Co(CO)3 has 9 + 3 × 2 = 15 VE and CH has 4 + 1 = 5 VE, so the cluster has 2 × 15 + 2 × 5 = 40 CVE (Co4(CO)12 itself has 4 × 15 = 60, and one substitution gives 50). The CH–CH unit can be viewed as an ethine (acetylene) molecule bound side-on to the two cobalt atoms.

prompt: Alkyne–dicobalt clusters can be made by treating Co2(CO)8 with an alkyne. What happens in this reaction?

choices.text: The alkyne donates its four π electrons to the cobalt atoms, two CO ligands are lost, and four Co–C bonds form
The alkyne donates two of its π electrons to cobalt, one CO ligand is lost, and two Co–C bonds form
choices.why: Both π bonds of the alkyne are used. Its four π electrons replace two CO ligands and give four Co–C bonds.

choices.text: Four CO ligands are lost, and the cobalt atoms rearrange into a tetrahedral Co4 cluster
choices.why: That is what heating Co2(CO)8 above 54 °C does on its own, giving Co4(CO)12. With an alkyne, the two Co atoms bond to the alkyne carbons.

choices.text: The C–C triple bond breaks right away, giving methine complexes that keep all eight CO ligands
choices.why: Under ordinary conditions the C–C bond stays intact. It can cleave to give methine complexes only under harsher conditions.

explanation: The view of 40 VE clusters as alkyne clusters is not just formal: they can be made from alkynes. The alkyne's four π electrons are donated into the cobalt d orbitals of Co2(CO)8, two CO ligands are lost, and four Co–C bonds form. Under harsher conditions the C–C bond can also cleave, giving access to methine complexes.

prompt: HCo(CO)4 is a strong acid, similar to sulfuric acid, but HMn(CO)5 is a weak acid, similar to H2S. Which explanation for the lower acidity of HMn(CO)5 does the section give?

choices.text: Losing H^+ would drop manganese's coordination number from the preferred 6 to 5
Losing H^+ would give a very stable 18 VE tetrahedral anion
choices.why: A very stable conjugate base makes an acid stronger, not weaker. That is the section's reason HCo(CO)4 is so acidic: losing H^+ gives the 18 VE tetrahedral Co(CO)4^− anion.

choices.text: Mn(CO)5 is not isolobal with a hydrogen atom, so a Mn–H bond is hard to break
choices.why: Mn(CO)5 is a 17 VE fragment with one frontier orbital holding one electron, so it is isolobal with H, whose frontier orbital is its 1s orbital.

choices.text: Its conjugate base, Mn(CO)5^−, would be only a 16 VE species with an empty frontier orbital
choices.why: Mn(CO)5^− has 7 + 1 + 5 × 2 = 18 VE. The section's argument for HMn(CO)5 is about coordination number.

explanation: A hydrogen atom has one frontier orbital, its 1s, with one electron, so it is isolobal with 17 VE fragments like Co(CO)4 and Mn(CO)5, and both carbonyl hydrides are stable. HCo(CO)4 loses its proton easily because that gives the very stable 18 VE tetrahedral Co(CO)4^− anion. For HMn(CO)5, losing the proton would reduce the coordination number from the preferred 6 to 5, so the tendency to lose it is small. The choice of metal, coordination number and other ligands L can tune carbonyl hydrides from highly acidic to hydridic.

prompt: Re(CO)5 is isolobal with CH3. Which of these fragments, with the same coordination number, is also isolobal with CH3?

choices.why: Removing an electron from Re(CO)5 gives a 16 VE fragment. By the section's rule, [Re(CO)5]^+ is isolobal with CH3^+, not CH3.

choices.text: Ru(CO)5
choices.why: Ru(CO)5 has 8 + 5 × 2 = 18 VE, so 18 − 18 = 0: it has no frontier orbital to match the one in CH3.
[Mo(CO)5]^+ has 6 − 1 + 5 × 2 = 15 VE and three frontier orbitals, like CH. The 17 VE CH3 analog is [Mo(CO)5]^−.

explanation: Isoelectronic fragments with the same coordination number are isolobal. Re(CO)5 has 7 + 5 × 2 = 17 VE, and [Ru(CO)5]^+ has 8 − 1 + 5 × 2 = 17 VE too, so it has one frontier orbital with one electron, like CH3. Any 17-electron fragment of this kind, including [Mo(CO)5]^−, is isolobal with CH3.

prompt: Square planar complexes typically follow the 16-electron rule, so the isolobal analogy needs an adjustment for them. Fe(CO)4 is a d^8 ML_4 fragment derived from an octahedron. Which fragment does the section's square planar rule relate to it?

choices.text: Pt(PR3)2, a d^10 ML_2 fragment
[PtCl4]^2−, a d^8 ML_4 complex
choices.why: This keeps both the number of ligands and the d count unchanged. The square planar analog has two fewer ligands and two more d electrons.

choices.text: [PtCl3]^−, a d^8 ML_3 fragment
choices.why: A d^8 ML_3 fragment corresponds to an octahedral d^6 ML_5 fragment, as [PdCl3]^− does to Mo(CO)5.

choices.text: Pt(PR3)4, a d^10 ML_4 fragment
choices.why: The d count correctly rises by two, but the number of ligands must also drop by two, from ML_4 to ML_2.

explanation: Assuming two-electron donor ligands, the metal in a square planar molecule is d^8. An octahedral fragment ML_n with a d^{x} metal relates to a square planar fragment ML_(n−2) with a d^(x+2) metal. For d^8 ML_4 Fe(CO)4, this gives a d^10 ML_2 fragment such as Pt(PR3)2, just as the section pairs d^8 Os(CO)4 with d^10 Ni(PR3)2.
